lines.watchItem: Leading-edge demand keeps running ahead of what the company can build: August revenue rose 53.3 percent against a year earlier, and its own quarterly demand for production tools now sits at roughly 1.9 times what was projected in December 2025 even while about twenty plants go up at once. Watch construction labour and equipment delivery, which are named as the pacing items rather than orders.

Advanced-packaging allocation is again described as the binding limit on whether finished systems reach buyers, with waits of roughly 52 to 78 weeks against capacity of about 105,000 to 130,000 wafers a month by the fourth quarter of 2026. The exposure is that packaging slots, not wafer starts, set how much accelerator revenue can actually be realised.

Advanced-packaging capacity is pre-booked at more than 85 percent for 2026 and 2027, with one buyer holding roughly 60 percent and the top three accounting for more than 85 percent. That concentration means a single large buyer trimming orders would leave slots that are hard to refill quickly.

The leading-node customer base is broadening from merchant accelerator vendors toward buyers designing their own parts: Microsoft is reported to be negotiating capacity for upward of 300,000 of its in-house accelerators for 2027 delivery, Meta is building its next in-house silicon with the company on production, and one model lab's first inference chip is built on a 3nm process. Watch whether this mix shift changes who books leading-node volume.

Pricing power across the chain stayed firm this cycle: the company posted a second-quarter 2026 gross margin of 67.7 percent with revenue up 36 percent and lifted full-year growth guidance above 40 percent, while the second-largest contract chipmaker raised prices 10 to 15 percent on new orders because it cannot meet all the orders it receives. The exposure is to how long that scarcity holds.

Memory costs are now eating into the accelerator vendors' own profitability, with the largest one guiding its coming quarter to 74.0 percent and citing a floor of 71 to 72 percent because memory prices rose more than it expected. Watch whether squeezed customer margins change how those buyers negotiate everything upstream of them.

A second-source packaging route is gaining real volume: Google has committed to order more than 3 million units of Intel's bridge packaging for a 2028 part, that process is reported above 90 percent yield at roughly half the cost of the company's own advanced packaging, and Intel holds about 13.7 percent of global 2.5D packaging capacity against the company's roughly 70 percent. Watch whether the reported cost gap pulls further work across.

Policy is the live variable on the demand the company serves: Washington is preparing tariffs on imported chips that would reach finished servers, with duty-free allowances sized to each company's United States fabrication investment and no rate or start date set, against the company's announced Arizona commitment now totalling 265 billion dollars. Watch how allowances are finally sized.
